newsitem.title: CHINA: China looks to social welfare as reform key.
newsitem.headline: China looks to social welfare as reform key.

text.p: China is turning to reform of its social welfare programmes as a key to shaking up its lumbering state industry without triggering unrest.

Beijing is dismantling the remnants of what once was a cradle-to-grave welfare system under Stalinist central planning. But it is also eyeing a greater role for the private sector in the hope of reducing the financial burden on the state.
"We believe the next step should be with the private sector," said Song Xiaowu, a specialist in pensions and medical insurance reform at the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy.
"We need insurance to supplement pension payments," he told Reuters in a recent interview, adding that private insurance companies could be allowed to insure employees of state corporations.
China has been trying to reform its retirement, medical and unemployment systems to relieve the financial strain on state corporations and the state itself.
State companies, saddled with debt and burdened with swollen payrolls, provide all benefits to their employees, meaning that a worker who loses his job stands to lose all of his benefits.
Beijing's cautious leaders see the prospect of armies of unemployed workers -- with no income or welfare benefits -- as a grave threat to stability.

Some 120 million urban workers are now covered under pension systems, though officials concede that there are vast gaps in the welfare system throughout the countryside where most of the population lives.

China has been moving slowly to replace its pay-as-you-go retirement scheme -- which pools contributions -- with a system of personal accounts that would enable workers take benefits as they move from one job to the next.
It wants to raise the contribution of the individual and lower the contribution from the state.

"A big problem now is that retirement systems are not uniform," said Song. "In the same city they may vary between a provincial government-owned company and a municipally-owned one. This makes it hard for people to take benefits from one job to another."
Authorities are moving toward a uniform plan that would have employees contribute about eight percent of their wages to be matched by three percent from the employer.
This could be supplemented by privately contracted insurance throught the workplace.
China has been expanding its insurance market, allowing new companies to enter the market, breaking up what had been a monopoly by the People's Insurance Group.
Song and other officials said that although China maintains it has only about three percent unemployment, much of its unemployment is not recorded.
Many employees are sent home with nothing to do, taking only a fraction of their salaries.
Comprehensive medical insurance has also proved elusive.
"We have great problems with medical insurance," said Song. "We can only say it is in an experimental stage in a few cities."
He said Shenzhen, the southern boomtown near Hong Kong, has experimented with a personal account for out-patient care with state funds covering in-hospital care.
